<Rep. Jared Huffman>: H.R. 2709, the Save Our Sequoias Act (SOS), provides a useful framework for organizing the federal response to the emergency conditions and restoration needs of giant sequoia groves. The bill was first introduced in response to several catastrophic wildfires that burned across Sequoia and Kings Canyon National Parks and the Sequoia National Forest, which led to the death of between 1,300 and 2,400 giant sequoias, or nearly 20 percent of the entire population.\1\
\1\National Park Service, Wildfires Kill Unprecedented Numbers of Large Sequoia Trees (July 18, 2023), Available online: https:// www.nps.gov/articles/000/wildfires-kill-unprecedented-numbers-of-large-sequoia-trees.htm.
The tragic loss of this iconic keystone species triggered a massive restoration effort aimed at promoting reforestation and reducing future wildfire risk. In fact, the Giant Sequoia Lands Coalition (GSLC) reported that 2024 was a landmark year for conservation work, with restoration and fuels-reduction efforts successfully completed across approximately 14,000 acres of sequoia groves and adjacent lands. While there is more work to be done across the approximately 80 individual groves, nearly half of the total grove acreage is already seeing vital intervention.\2\
\2\Giant Sequoia Lands Coalition, 2024 Progress Report: Saving Our Giants (May 13, 2025), Available online: https:// www.savetheredwoods.org/wp-content/uploads/files/PR-20250513_2024-GSLC- Annual-Report.pdf.
H.R. 2709 presents an opportunity to support ongoing emergency efforts. However, as introduced, SOS would have aggressively waived or altered environmental compliance standards, including the National Environmental Policy Act, the Endangered Species Act, and the National Historic Preservation Act. These bedrock environmental laws help guide federal projects, balance multiple objectives, and achieve long-term sustainability.
Acknowledging these concerns, Committee Republicans and the bill sponsors negotiated in good faith to improve the bill. The amendment in the nature of a substitute (ANS) filed by Chair Westerman incorporates significant guardrails, including requirements that all ``Protection Projects'' comply with existing land management plans and federal laws, meet public notice and meeting requirements, and abide by ``extraordinary circumstances'' protections when carrying out Categorical Exclusions (CEs) authorized by the bill. Additionally, the ANS removes amendments to the Wilderness Act and Endangered Species Act carve-outs for specific species.
The changes incorporated into the ANS reflect a stronger, more balanced piece of legislation better equipped to support the ongoing restoration and recovery of our giant sequoias. As climate-driven wildfires threaten their very existence, this legislation provides focused, species-specific tools to facilitate the ongoing, coordinated response. Furthermore, the ANS demonstrates that through bipartisan negotiations the committee can find balanced approaches to forest and wildfire management that has been lacking in other legislation considered in this Congress.
However, this bill is just one piece of the puzzle. Our federal land management agencies, including the National Park Service and the U.S. Forest Service, require adequate funding and staffing to fulfill their congressionally mandated missions. The survival of one of America's most extraordinary natural icons is at stake. If the story of the giant sequoias tells us anything, it is that Congress must take seriously its responsibility to support and steward our national parks, forests, and public lands.
Jared Huffman,
Ranking Member.
